title: LSASS handle and memory dump produced by Windows Error Reporting

alert.rule_name: Credential Access: LSASS Process Memory Read via Suspicious Handle

mitre_attack.technique: T1003.001 - OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory

alert.description: A process obtained a handle to lsass.exe with access rights permitting memory reads (PROCESS_VM_READ). LSASS holds plaintext credentials, hashes, and Kerberos tickets in memory; non-security-tooling reads of LSASS are a high-fidelity indicator of credential theft, independent of the dumping tool used.
alert.detection_logic: Sysmon EventID=10 (ProcessAccess) WHERE TargetImage ENDSWITH '\lsass.exe' AND GrantedAccess IN (0x1010,0x1038,0x1410,0x1438,0x143a,0x1fffff) AND SourceImage NOT IN (known_security_tooling) AND SourceImage NOT IN (wininit.exe, csrss.exe, services.exe, MsMpEng.exe)

enrichment.wer_mechanism: Windows Error Reporting handles application crashes. When a process faults, the WER service (WerSvc, hosted in svchost.exe) launches WerFault.exe with the crashing process's PID, and WerFault opens a handle to that process to capture a memory snapshot for the crash report. Producing a memory dump of the faulting process is the entire purpose of the tool.
enrichment.command_line_form: WerFault.exe -pss -s 468 -p 756 -ip 756 is the standard snapshot invocation: -p and -ip identify the target process (756 = lsass.exe), -s is the shared-memory handle the service passed in, and -pss requests a process snapshot. The PID on the command line was supplied by the service, not chosen by a user.
enrichment.crash_precedes_handle: The Application Error record for lsass.exe is timestamped 0.151 seconds BEFORE the ProcessAccess alert. The ordering matters: the handle is a consequence of the crash. In a credential-theft case the handle comes first and no crash is recorded at all.
enrichment.call_trace_note: The alerting CallTrace resolves entirely to signed, on-disk Microsoft modules (ntdll.dll, KERNEL32.DLL, dbgcore.DLL, faultrep.dll). There is no UNKNOWN frame and no unbacked memory, so no reflectively-loaded code participated in the read.
enrichment.identity_and_parent: WerFault.exe runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM at System integrity, in terminal session 0, with svchost.exe -k WerSvcGroup as its parent. No interactive user account and no user session appears anywhere in the chain.
enrichment.dump_location: The dump was written to C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\WER\ReportQueue\AppCrash_lsass.exe_9f2b4c1e7a3d\lsass.exe.756.dmp — the standard WER report queue, a system-managed directory that WER creates, populates and later purges. Contrast a user-writable staging path such as AppData\Local\Temp.
enrichment.report_closure: The Windows Error Reporting record 1001 that follows names the same Report Id as the crash record and lists the same dump path as an attached file, closing the loop between crash, dump and report.

verdict.rationale: The provided chain is internally consistent with Windows Error Reporting handling an LSASS crash: an Application Error precedes WerSvc startup, svchost launches WerFault as SYSTEM with a process-snapshot command line for LSASS PID 756, WerFault creates a dump in the WER ReportQueue while opening LSASS, and Application event 1001 records that same dump as an APPCRASH attachment. This explains the alert without requiring credential-dumping intent, while the dump remains sensitive operational data.

inferences.desc: The ordering and shared LSASS PID indicate that WerFault's process access and dump creation were consequences of the recorded LSASS crash.

The service parent, snapshot arguments, fault-reporting module, ReportQueue path, and APPCRASH closure together form a coherent Windows Error Reporting workflow rather than an unexplained LSASS-memory read.
Credential-theft intent is not supported by the provided chain, though the resulting LSASS dump contains sensitive process memory.

investigations.desc: If the LSASS crash recurs, investigate host reliability and the faulting msv1_0.DLL condition separately from this security alert.
Verify that WER retention and access controls protect or remove the LSASS dump because it contains sensitive memory.
Review telemetry immediately before the crash if assurance is needed that the fault was not deliberately induced.
Check for access to or transfer of the dump after creation beyond the provided event chain if data-handling risk must be excluded.

unknowns.desc: The root cause of the LSASS crash and whether it was naturally occurring or deliberately induced are unknown.
Access to, retention of, or transfer of the dump after the provided event chain is unknown.
